title: Thyatira (Revelation 2:18–29)
hook: their latest works are more than their first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pergamum, and a white stone with a name on it that nobody else can read. Your line was a new name. Did the stone in your pocket remind you of anything? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

By a riverside outside the city of Philippi, Paul sits down with some women who have gathered to pray. One of them, the book of Acts says, is "a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira." A businesswoman far from home. She listens, and the text says the Lord opened her heart. Her home town is today's word. Revelation's next letter goes to the church in Thyatira, and the voice that speaks is fierce: eyes "like unto a flame of fire," feet like fine brass. You'd brace for a scolding. Instead, the first thing he says is a compliment worth framing. This church is getting better.

First, the praise, in the King James words: "I know thy works, and charity, and service, and faith, and thy patience, and thy works; and the last to be more than the first." Charity is the King James word here for love. And notice the end. Three days ago, the church in Ephesus heard that it had left its first love. Thyatira hears the reverse: what they're doing now is more than what they did at the start. Their faith is growing, not fading. Second, the trouble. The letter says they put up with a teacher it calls "that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess." The letter doesn't give her real name. Jezebel reaches back to the queen in the book of Kings, wife of King Ahab, who served Baal. The complaint is about what she taught: eating food sacrificed to idols and what the letter calls fornication. And even here there's patience. "I gave her space to repent," the voice says. Third, a word to everyone else in the church who didn't follow that teaching: "I will put upon you none other burden. But that which ye have already hold fast till I come." No new load. Just keep hold of what you've got. Fourth, the promise at the end: "And I will give him the morning star." A light that shows before dawn. Put together, Thyatira is a church with a real problem in its middle, and still the first thing heaven says to it is that it's growing. The letter doesn't treat growth as a peak you hit at the start and slide down from. It treats it as something that can keep going, a little more each season.
screen: `I WILL GIVE HIM THE MORNING STAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do better than yesterday. Settle, and breathe. Let yesterday play back slowly, like a film. Stop it at one ordinary moment you'd do a little differently. A short answer to someone. A meal eaten standing up. A chance to help that went by. No need for a whole new life; just one notch better. Picture today's version of that moment, done with a bit more care. If you pray, you can offer that moment to God and ask for help with it. If you don't, just hold the picture, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Thyatira. Lydia's home town, and the church told that its latest works were more than its first, even with a real problem in its middle.
Your line: more than at first. Today, do one ordinary thing a little better than you did it yesterday: the dishes, the reply, the hello at the door. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Christians speak of growing in faith over a lifetime, and some make a habit of looking back over each day in prayer to notice what went well and what could be done better tomorrow.

fork.reveal: the letter opens with praise: "the last to be more than the first." the warning comes after.

original.note: Greek: love. the word the King James renders 'charity' in Revelation 2:19.

trapdoor: what you thought: Thyatira is a letter about a woman called Jezebel.
what it means: it opens with praise for a church whose later works are more than its first, then names a real problem.
what a scholar hears: the name Jezebel reaches back to the queen of the book of Kings, and Thyatira is also Lydia's home town in Acts 16:14.

notes: The review refers back to Ephesus ('three days ago') and its 'first love' (Revelation 2:4), taught on day 1290. Confirm day 1290 is the Ephesus letter in the final order.

'Jezebel' is described as a name for the teacher reaching back to the queen of Kings; the letter gives no other name. Confirm the handling, and that the lesson keeps the complaint on her teaching (2:20), not on her being a woman.
'Charity here is the old English word for love' (ἀγάπη in 2:19). Confirm.
howItsDone mentions a daily look back in prayer (e.g. an examen); confirm the wording is fair across churches.
Editor pass: dropped the 'old English word' etymology claim; tied Jezebel to the text of 1 Kings 16:31 (Ahab's wife; Baal worship); softened the morning-star gloss.
